slides.title: Why Open Data Center for AI, Why Now
slides.subtitle: See which facility decisions determine whether the next rack generation can arrive, connect, and operate without redesign.

source_refs.source: OCP Open Data Center for AI Whitepaper FINAL.pdf

slides.transcript:
Welcome to Open Data Center for AI. The expensive question is no longer whether a facility can support today's rack. It is whether the next rack—heavier, denser, and possibly from a different supplier—can move from dock to row, land on the floor, connect to power and cooling, and operate without a redesign.

Revision 0.7 turns those risks into measurable facility interfaces. By the end of this course, you will know which constraints to test first, which capacity figures belong at rack, row, or hall level, and where the specification deliberately protects implementation choice. The specification is our technical center of gravity, with context from the OCP strategic initiative and its EMEA Summit discussion, including perspectives from AMD, Google, Meta, and NVIDIA.

slides.transcript:
The course follows the logic of a real facility decision. In four modules, you will gain a review lens you can use before committing capital. You will learn which physical constraints can stop a dense rack before it reaches the row; where power and cooling numbers actually apply; why a full-row manifold and a rack connector are different decisions; and how to compare implementation options without mistaking an example for a requirement.

Allow about forty-five minutes for narration, study, and the scenario checks. This edition uses published Revision 0.7, effective August twenty-seventh, twenty twenty-six. The specification link and a reusable review worksheet are included. The worksheet helps you record evidence and open questions; it is not an engineering approval.

slides.title: One Rack Change Reaches Beyond the Rack

figure.alt: One rack is exchanged in a physical row; power, liquid circuits and service clearance are traced before a wider hall is revealed. Liquid pipes use blue for supply and red for return.
figure.caption: Teaching model: a rack change propagates through power, cooling, space and hall planning. Geometry is illustrative; source concepts are available in the specification Appendix. Pipe key: blue = cooler supply; red = warmer return.

slides.transcript:
Start with the rack in the foreground. A different accelerator system arrives. Its power demand, liquid flow, weight, or maintenance needs can differ even when the nominal rack width looks familiar.

Follow the electrical path upward to the row busways. More distribution hardware still needs adequate upstream supply. Now follow the liquid supply and return. The row manifold and each branch must support the equipment's flow and operating conditions. Finally, look at the aisle and overhead space. A system that connects can still be impossible to move or maintain.

As the view opens to the hall, these are no longer isolated rack decisions. They affect shared electrical and thermal infrastructure and ultimately the utility connection. This is the whitepaper's system-level idea: the facility becomes part of the computer. Early interface planning reduces late surprises, but every candidate system still needs verification.

slides.title: From a Google Reference to a Shared Industry Baseline
slides.subtitle: The technical center of gravity moved from one deployment model to common requirements for industry AI/ML systems.

bullets.text: AMD, Google, Meta, and NVIDIA now author the unified guidance.
The scope centers on next-generation AI and machine-learning facility requirements.
Structural, power, cooling, and interface targets replace many platform-specific prescriptions.
Rigid row lengths give way to kilowatts per linear foot.
Google-specific near-term tables, TPU scaling, campus layouts, and the 10%-38% humidity limit are removed.

figure.alt: Timeline from the Google-authored 0.5 specification to the AMD, Google, Meta, and NVIDIA 0.7 collaboration.
figure.caption: Revision 0.5 is the earlier Google-authored baseline. Revision 0.7 lists AMD, Google, Meta and NVIDIA; it is not the specification’s first release.

slides.transcript:
Revision zero point five was an important Google-authored reference. Revision 0.7 becomes a broader industry baseline, with AMD, Google, Meta, and NVIDIA listed as authors. That added collaboration matters because the target is no longer one operator's near-term layout. It is a common envelope for multiple AI and ML systems expected across twenty twenty-seven and twenty twenty-eight.

The revision history shows the shift. Platform-specific tables, fixed row-length prescriptions, campus layouts, and several older appendices were removed. In their place, the document emphasizes first-principles targets for structure, space, power, cooling, and interfaces. The new revision also expresses row capacity in modular kilowatts per linear foot. The result is more concise, but it asks the reader to preserve context carefully: a stable requirement is not the same thing as a mandated physical solution.

slides.title: Fungibility Depends on Standard Interfaces
slides.subtitle: Compatibility at the boundaries gives each implementation room to innovate.

figure.alt: Two different rack implementations are tested against the same separately named physical, power and liquid requirements.
figure.caption: Shared review criteria do not make different connectors or equipment automatically interchangeable. Each proposed system still needs evidence at the boundary.

entries.text: Shared targets preserve choice; each system still needs evidence.

source_refs.source: OCP Open Data Center for AI Whitepaper FINAL.pdf

slides.transcript:
These two rack implementations are deliberately different. Fungibility does not require matching internals. It means the facility can accommodate different systems and generations with limited retrofit.

Hold the review boundary steady: structural and moving loads, physical clearances, power delivery, liquid operating conditions, and service access. Then require evidence from each proposed implementation. A matching nominal envelope is useful, but it does not prove that plugs, fluid connections, or operating agreements match.

This is what makes late binding practical. The site can advance before the final accelerator decision, while unresolved interfaces remain visible. The wider strategic initiative also addresses telemetry and service-level agreements. These are continuing coordination needs, not a promise that Revision 0.7 already defines a universal connection for everything.

slides.transcript:
The Open Data Center specification is one part of a wider OCP strategic initiative. The first workstream develops open facility reference designs for power, cooling, mechanical systems, and row infrastructure. That is where Revision 0.7 contributes most directly.

Four other workstreams extend the system view. Energy and grid work addresses connection requirements, flexibility, on-site generation, and storage. Open service-level agreements create shared engineering practices among facilities, equipment, and workload operators. Telemetry work seeks secure, harmonized observations across IT and operational technology. Power estimation improves planning when workload behavior and silicon roadmaps are uncertain. Together, the five streams connect the building, the grid, the hardware, and operations. A good facility envelope is necessary, but it creates full value only when these adjacent agreements and measurements mature with it.

Stable interfaces support fungibility, faster deployment, and stronger supply-chain alignment.
Reference designs are one workstream within a wider Open Data Center for AI initiative.

slides.title: The Facility Compatibility Envelope
slides.subtitle: Coordinate what the facility must carry, clear, connect, and adapt
slides.transcript:
Module two is the Facility Compatibility Envelope. The question is not merely whether a rack fits in its final position. The facility must carry it, move it, clear it, connect it, and remain adaptable as equipment generations change.

We will translate Revision 0.7 into an end-to-end physical review, from the structural load basis and moving load to row dimensions and the overhead coordination zone.

slides.title: Facility Constraints You Will Translate
slides.subtitle: By the end of this module, you will be able to:
objectives: Interpret the rack and sidecar structural load bases.
Coordinate row dimensions with safe equipment movement.
Apply the ceiling and overhead-infrastructure requirements.
Explain why Revision 0.7.0 replaces fixed row lengths with modular density.
slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, you should be able to review the total moving load, interpret the row dimensions and their measurement points, and check overhead space for the chosen services.

Keep the forty-eight-inch structural depth basis separate from Table one's seventy-one-inch row-envelope target. The table is headed minimum dimensions; we will not silently reinterpret that target as a maximum. We will also distinguish a source recommendation from a requirement.

slides.title: A Rack That Fits Can Still Fail to Arrive

figure.alt: A rack and power sidecar on transport equipment stop at a dock leveler, doorway and turn, then a lift before reaching the row.
figure.caption: 8,000 lb rack + 7,000 lb sidecar = 15,000 lb before handling equipment. Each route checkpoint needs its own load, clearance and swept-envelope review; this is not a structural approval.

entries.text: Stop and verify at every route boundary

slides.transcript:
The specification's heaviest-rack design target is eight thousand pounds over a twenty-eight by forty-eight inch structural basis. Its rack-and-sidecar example adds seven thousand pounds to eight thousand: fifteen thousand pounds before the handling equipment.

Watch the transporter stop at the dock leveler. Review the actual moving load and concentrated wheel loads, not just the stationary rack footprint. At the doorway and turn, check the loaded swept envelope, not only the rack width. At the lift, the platform size and applicable load rating both matter. None of those checks is replaced by a suitable final-row floor.

The panel emphasized these ordinary deployment blockers. The animation shows where to ask the questions, not a certified transporter or route. The actual equipment, load distribution, handling method, and local structure still require qualified review.

slides.title: Keep Each Dimension Attached to Its Datum
slides.subtitle: The structural footprint and the deployable row envelope answer different questions.

figure.alt: Dimensioned plan and elevation separating aisle clearances, rack-envelope targets and structural footprint.
figure.caption: Table 1 is headed “Minimum dimensions” and lists 71 in rack depth and 100 in height. These are row-envelope targets here—not an invented maximum. Section 4.2 calls 12 ft transport clearance a recommendation; Table 1 lists it among minimums.

slides.transcript:
Keep each dimension attached to its datum. Table one lists a fifty-four-inch hot aisle and an eighty-two-inch cold aisle, the latter measured from IT rack face to face. It also lists a one-hundred-inch rack-height target and a seventy-one-inch rack-depth target under its minimum-dimensions heading.

Those row-envelope targets are separate from the forty-eight-inch depth used in the structural load example. Do not relabel seventy-one inches as a maximum without clarification from the authors.

There is another wording distinction. Section four point two calls twelve feet of transport clearance a design recommendation; Table one lists twelve feet among minimum dimensions. Preserve both statements and resolve their application in the project review. The recommended twenty-four-foot aisle pitch and the Appendix row plan provide further context; the drawing does not override the core text.

slides.title: Measure to the Beam—Not the Ceiling Finish

figure.alt: A cutaway measures a fixed 18-foot floor-to-beam datum, exposes the air plenum, then compares a separate higher-clearance design. Liquid pipes use blue for supply and red for return.
figure.caption: Section 4.2: two-busway configuration, 18 ft minimum from floor to beam underside, including the plenum. Additional busways and tray tiers may need more height; the second view is a different design, not a moving building beam. Pipe key: blue = cooler supply; red = warmer return.

slides.transcript:
The fixed vertical datum runs from the floor to the underside of the structural beam. For a two-busway configuration, Section four point two requires at least eighteen feet, including the air-plenum space. It is not a measurement to the ceiling finish.

The cutaway exposes why that distinction matters. Racks and containment sit below power distribution, liquid piping, cable routing, and the air-return volume. Fire protection, lighting, and maintenance also need coordination, even when a simplified view omits their detail.

Now compare a separate design with additional busways and tray tiers. The eighteen-foot reference stays fixed; the second arrangement may need a higher beam. This is a design comparison, not a suggestion to lift an existing building beam. For constrained sites, the source calls for custom design variations, supported by the relevant engineering review.

slides.title: Changing Row Length Changes Capacity

figure.alt: Two distinct fixed-building layouts show different available row lengths, with a continuous length datum and an illustrative linear-density calculation. Liquid pipes use blue for supply and red for return.
figure.caption: Illustrative arithmetic at an assumed uniform 25 kW/ft: 40 ft × 25 = 1,000 kW; 32 ft × 25 = 800 kW. This teaches units, not a required row length or a complete blended-facility capacity model. Pipe key: blue = cooler supply; red = warmer return.

entries.text: Linear row length · schematic, not to scale

slides.transcript:
The building columns stay fixed. What changes is the proposed row arrangement. Revision 0.7 replaces rigid row-length prescriptions with modular density in kilowatts per linear foot.

Use an illustrative calculation to see the units. At an assumed uniform twenty-five kilowatts per foot, forty usable feet correspond to one thousand kilowatts. If the available row is thirty-two feet, the same assumed density gives eight hundred kilowatts. Neither length is a specification requirement, and this simple arithmetic is not a complete blended-facility capacity model.

The second design accommodates a different equipment mix and site geometry. Shortening the row does not make the lost capacity disappear. Reconcile the actual length, equipment demand, power, cooling, access, and structural conditions before accepting the arrangement.

slides.title: The Facility Must Carry, Clear, and Adapt
items: The heaviest-rack target is 8,000 lb, while the rack-plus-sidecar moving-load example reaches 15,000 lb before handling equipment.
Docks, doors, lifts, floor routes, and placement tools belong in the same movement analysis.
Minimum row dimensions coordinate hot aisle, cold aisle, rack depth and height, and transport access.
Two-busway configurations require an 18 ft minimum ceiling height; denser overhead systems may require more.
Modular kW/ft guidance replaces fixed row lengths so the design can evolve with power and fluid connections.
slides.transcript:
Review the whole route, not just the final rack position. Fifteen thousand pounds excludes the handling equipment. Clearance includes doors, turns, lifts, aisles, and service access.

For the two-busway overhead reference, measure floor to beam underside and include the plenum. Preserve Table one's wording where its targets need clarification. Modular density changes how row length is planned, not the need to verify actual capacity.

slides.title: Power and Cooling at AI Density
slides.subtitle: Use the right density measure at the right level of the facility
slides.transcript:
Module three examines Power and Cooling at AI Density. The central discipline is to use the right number at the right level.

A blended value describes a mixed facility. A peak value protects the most demanding local zone. Cluster megawatts, hall power blocks, row busways, cooling splits, pipe diameters, and quick connects are related, but they are not interchangeable. We will keep each target attached to its scope and assumptions.

slides.title: Capacity Targets You Will Interpret
slides.subtitle: By the end of this module, you will be able to:
objectives: Distinguish blended data-center density from peak IT density.
Recall the cluster and data-hall power targets in Revision 0.7.0.
Explain what the specification fixes and leaves flexible in power distribution.
Use cooling-density and manifold-flow values without dropping their qualifications.
slides.transcript:
Use the right number at the right level. In this module, distinguish the mixed-facility baseline from a local peak, separate hall block count from row distribution, and interpret a liquid-capacity screen under its stated flow assumptions.

The review question is not which number is largest. It is which number governs the equipment and interface you are actually evaluating.

slides.title: Peak and Blended Density Answer Different Questions

figure.alt: A mixed equipment row is contrasted with one local high-density rack zone; the highlighted area is not a numerical proportion.
figure.caption: The mixed-facility baseline and local peak protect different planning boundaries. Schematic only: box area is not a peak-zone percentage, and the peak is not a uniform load on every row.

slides.transcript:
The mixed equipment view includes machine learning, network, general compute, and storage. Blended density describes that planning mix. Peak IT density protects the highest-powered machine-learning rack condition in a local high-density zone.

Revision 0.7 gives a twenty-five-kilowatt-per-foot blended baseline and a three-hundred-fifty-kilowatt-per-foot peak IT target. The document separately identifies an expected twenty twenty-seven rack peak of one hundred twenty-five kilowatts per foot.

The highlighted area is schematic; it is not a specified percentage of the hall. Do not apply the largest peak uniformly to every row, and do not average it away where demanding racks will be installed. Map the actual equipment mix and local demand, then size the relevant supply and cooling paths.

slides.title: The 0.7 Capacity Targets in One View
slides.subtitle: Preserve the level and context attached to each number.
rows: Air-cooled share within the blended design
Liquid capacity supporting the blended design
slides.transcript:
Here is the capacity model in one view. The blended data-center baseline is twenty-five kilowatts per linear foot, or eighty-two kilowatts per meter. Within that design, the specified capabilities are fifteen kilowatts per linear foot of air cooling and twenty-five kilowatts per linear foot of liquid cooling. These are capabilities, not a statement that their full values are always additive at every location.

For the near horizon, the document identifies an expected twenty twenty-seven rack peak of one hundred twenty-five kilowatts per linear foot. The broader peak IT target is three hundred fifty kilowatts per linear foot. At the cluster level, plan for twelve megawatts minimum and twenty-four megawatts preferred. Preserve these labels when the numbers move into requirements, models, or presentations. A value without its level and context can create a confidently wrong design.

slides.title: Four Power Blocks Is a Hall Minimum

figure.alt: A hall contains four correctly proportioned power blocks; a separate row detail compares two and four overhead busways without assigning blocks to fixed zones.
figure.caption: Section 5.2 specifies at least four blocks per hall. Block ratings, independence, redundancy and row mapping are not defined there. More busways do not create more upstream power.

entries.text: ≥ 4 per hall · ratings and topology require the design

slides.transcript:
Count the power blocks at hall level. Section five point two requires at least four. That sentence does not define a block's megawatt rating, independent feeds, redundancy, or a mandatory one-block-to-one-row mapping. Those details need the actual electrical design.

Now move to the separate row detail. Two busways and four busways are different distribution arrangements. Their number depends on the design and desired row power density. Adding busways does not create upstream power or prove independent supplies.

The Appendix drawings help visualize routing and equipment, but they are examples. Keep three records distinct: the hall's minimum block count, the available supply and topology, and the row's distribution and connection design. Component specifications can support that review; they do not remove the need to connect these levels.

slides.title: Keep Blended Capability Separate From the Peak

figure.alt: A connected liquid supply-and-return circuit serves physical racks while a distinct residual-air path remains visible; one local peak zone is highlighted. Liquid pipes use blue for supply and red for return.
figure.caption: Blended planning by 2028: 25 kW/ft liquid and 15 kW/ft air capabilities—not a universal 40 kW/ft operating load. At the local 350 kW/ft peak condition, the stated split is 335 liquid + 15 air. Pipe key: blue = cooler supply; red = warmer return.

slides.transcript:
Follow the liquid supply into the row, through the equipment branches, and back along the return. The connected circuit matters: floating drops do not explain a cooling system. The separate air path remains visible because liquid-cooled installations can still include air-cooled equipment.

For blended planning by twenty twenty-eight, the source calls for up to twenty-five kilowatts per foot of liquid capability and fifteen of air capability. These are separately named capabilities, not a universal forty-kilowatt-per-foot operating load.

Now focus on the local high-density zone. At the three-hundred-fifty-kilowatt-per-foot peak condition, Section six point three states three hundred thirty-five liquid plus fifteen air. That split belongs to the peak case, not the entire row by default. The physical loop shown is illustrative; the actual flow, temperatures, pressure losses, and equipment interfaces need engineering verification.

slides.title: The Same Pipe Can Pass One Screen and Fail Another
slides.subtitle: Table 3 calculates maximum cooling at a stated fluid speed of 3 m/s.

figure.alt: At a fixed illustrative 300 kW liquid load, a two-inch path is compared at the two Table 3 flow ratios; the row backbone and separate rack branches are then distinguished. Liquid pipes use blue for supply and red for return.
figure.caption: Illustrative 300 kW capacity screen at Table 3’s 3 m/s assumption: a 2 in path gives 365 kW at 1 lpm/kW, but 243 kW at 1.5 lpm/kW. Neither result approves the actual hydraulic design or connector. Pipe key: blue = cooler supply; red = warmer return.

slides.transcript:
Consider an illustrative three-hundred-kilowatt liquid load. Keep the row and the two-inch flow path fixed. Table three assumes a fluid speed of three meters per second.

At one liter per minute per kilowatt, the table gives three hundred sixty-five kilowatts of capacity: above this illustrative load. If the equipment instead requires one point five liters per minute per kilowatt, the same diameter gives only two hundred forty-three kilowatts. That screen fails. The pipe has not become shorter; the required flow per kilowatt has increased.

Next, distinguish the full-row backbone from the individual rack branches. A larger manifold does not mean its entire flow passes through one smaller rack connector. The published August twenty twenty-six specification notes a two-inch quick-connect availability limit; verify actual hardware for the project. Use the complete table and assumptions in the linked ledger. Even a passing capacity screen still needs pressure-loss, fluid, temperature, and connector validation.

slides.title: Capacity Planning Must Join Power and Thermal Design
items: Blended density describes the whole data-center mix; peak density protects the highest-powered local zone.
Revision 0.7.0 sets a 25 kW/ft blended baseline and a 350 kW/ft peak-IT target.
The cluster baseline is 12 MW minimum and 24 MW preferred.
Each data hall provides at least four power blocks, while busway count per row remains design-specific.
Cooling splits, row-manifold sizing, flow ratio, and quick-connect availability must be interpreted together.
slides.transcript:
Keep four boundaries distinct: mixed-facility planning, local peak demand, hall power architecture, and the actual row-to-rack connection.

Four power blocks is a minimum count, not a redundancy specification. Liquid capacity depends on the flow assumptions, and a larger row manifold does not approve an individual connector. Carry those distinctions into the next two review decisions.

slides.title: Apply 0.7 Without Freezing Innovation
slides.subtitle: Turn the requirement set into a repeatable design and review practice
slides.transcript:
Module four is about applying Revision 0.7 without freezing innovation. A useful standard makes projects more compatible and predictable. It should not turn one contributor's reference concept into the only valid building design.

We will use the boundary between the normative core and the non-normative Appendix to create a disciplined, auditable workflow for site-specific decisions.

slides.title: Decisions You Will Make With the Specification
slides.subtitle: By the end of this module, you will be able to:
objectives: Separate normative requirements from non-normative Appendix concepts.
Use common interfaces without treating one example as the only valid design.
Adapt implementation choices to regional and site constraints.
Run a concise Revision 0.7.0 compatibility review and identify follow-on resources.
slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, you should be able to use Appendix concepts without treating them as requirements, distinguish shared targets from project-specific interfaces, and document an unresolved site variation.

The goal is a traceable review: source, site condition, proposed response, evidence, owner, and disposition. A plausible drawing is the start of that conversation, not its approval.

slides.title: Compare One Design Choice at a Time

figure.alt: A physical rack line compares a rear fanwall with in-row coolers occupying real gaps, then separately compares busway count and overhead space.
figure.caption: Teaching comparison informed by Google and NVIDIA Appendix concepts (pp. 12–16). Cooling placement and busway count are separate choices. Service access and overhead clearances must be rechecked for each proposed arrangement.

entries.text: Service aisle stays in front of the equipment

slides.transcript:
First compare cooling placement while the busway arrangement stays unchanged. A rear fanwall and in-row coolers use space differently. In-row units occupy real positions in the rack line; they cannot simply cover the rack fronts. Service access and air paths need to remain workable.

Then compare busway count separately. Additional busways and tray tiers can change the overhead coordination problem. Recheck the height; do not assume that different arrangements fit the same volume.

The Google and NVIDIA Appendix concepts provide useful reference views for these questions. They are non-normative examples, not mandatory construction details. The course animation separates the design variables to make the tradeoffs visible; it does not certify a combined design. Return to the core text and the actual site evidence for each acceptance decision.

slides.title: Compatibility Must Be Demonstrated

figure.alt: Different rack systems are evaluated separately for physical fit, electrical connection, liquid connection and operational agreement; no universal docking connector is depicted. Liquid pipes use blue for supply and red for return.
figure.caption: Conceptual review model, not a universal connector standard. The 0.7 baseline sets selected facility targets; telemetry and operating agreements also depend on broader initiative work and project-specific engineering. Pipe key: blue = cooler supply; red = warmer return.

entries.text: Verify each candidate’s envelope and movement route
The actual fluid interface must be validated
OPERATING AGREEMENTS: define owners and evidence

slides.transcript:
Different rack systems can be evaluated against the same facility targets without sharing an identical connector. Start with the physical boundary: weight, movement, envelope, and access. Then examine the electrical connection, rating, and supply arrangement. Next check the liquid connection, required flow, pressure, and temperature conditions.

The second system may need a different implementation or a documented adaptation. That is not automatic failure, but it is also not plug-and-play proof. Each boundary requires evidence and a responsible reviewer.

Finally, agree on service responsibilities and operating information. Telemetry and service-level agreements belong to the broader initiative and project coordination; Revision 0.7 does not fully specify universal interfaces for them. This is a conceptual review model, not a new standardized docking product.

slides.title: A Site Variation Needs an Evidence Record

figure.alt: A filled review record for an illustrative 17-foot-six-inch floor-to-beam site records the source requirement, proposed custom design, evidence, owner and unresolved disposition.
figure.caption: Illustrative case, not an approved exception: a 17 ft 6 in site needs a custom design under §4.2. The MEP lead coordinates clearance, thermal, structural, fire and maintenance evidence with accountable reviewers. Status remains OPEN until resolved.

entries.text: §4.2 · 18 ft floor to beam · two busways
17 ft 6 in measured floor to beam
Clearance, plenum, thermal, structure, fire, access
OPEN · required reviews and acceptance pending

slides.transcript:
Consider a site with seventeen feet six inches from floor to beam underside. The proposed two-busway arrangement is below the eighteen-foot reference in Section four point two. That section explicitly calls for custom design variations where facilities cannot meet the standard.

The review record therefore names the source and datum, records the measured site condition, and describes a proposed custom overhead arrangement. The evidence must address clearances, the air plenum, thermal performance, structural implications, fire protection, and maintenance access. The MEP lead coordinates those reviews with the accountable specialists and operator.

The status is open. An Appendix picture and a claim of equivalent intent do not complete the review. Use the linked worksheet to record assumptions, evidence, owners, and unresolved approvals. This is an illustrative case, not an approved exception or blanket permission to vary other requirements.

slides.title: Use 0.7 as a Living Design Baseline
slides.subtitle: A concise review keeps authority, interfaces, and assumptions visible.

cards.title: 1. Confirm authority
cards.body: Use the published 0.7 core, dated August 27, 2026. Preserve the wording of requirements, recommendations and targets; keep Appendix examples separate.

cards.title: 2. Verify movement
cards.body: Check rack, sidecar, handling equipment, docks, doors, lifts, routes, and floor capacity.

cards.title: 3. Map the row
cards.body: Coordinate rack envelope, aisle clearances, pitch, overhead space, and service access.

cards.title: 4. Size capacity
cards.body: Apply blended and peak density at the correct levels; join power and thermal planning.

cards.title: 5. Document interfaces
cards.body: Record physical, electrical and fluid evidence. Identify project-specific telemetry and operational agreements separately from defined 0.7 targets.

cards.title: 6. Track evolution
cards.body: Revisit the baseline as the specification, regional rules, and equipment roadmaps change.

Use the worksheet to join six review areas: source authority, equipment movement, row geometry, capacity, interface evidence, and version control.

Record the published specification date alongside its requirements, recommendations, and targets. Keep project-specific telemetry and operating agreements distinct from what 0.7 actually defines. Give each open item an owner and required evidence. Revisit the record when the site, equipment, or source changes. The useful outcome is a visible decision trail—not a checklist of unexplained green ticks.

slides.title: A Repeatable Path From Specification to Facility
items: The normative core defines requirements; the Appendix provides non-normative design concepts.
Common interfaces protect compatibility while implementation details remain open.
Site and regional constraints require explicit, documented engineering choices.
A sound review joins structure, conveyance, row geometry, power, cooling, and operations.
Revision 0.7.0 is a living baseline supported by broader OCP work on energy, telemetry, SLAs, and power estimation.
